laws.title: Hands-Free Driving Law
laws.subtitle: AS 28.35.161 — No handheld devices while driving
laws.fullDescription: Alaska prohibits holding or using a handheld electronic device while operating a motor vehicle. Drivers must use Bluetooth or speakerphone without holding the device. Hands-free accessories are required.
laws.penalty: $500 fine for first offense, increasing for subsequent violations.
laws.exceptions: Emergency calls to 911, law enforcement, or fire/medical services are exempt.

quiz.q: What is Alaska's fine for a first handheld phone offense while driving?
quiz.explanation: Alaska's first offense fine for handheld device use while driving is $500.

laws.title: Non-Resident Hunting & Fishing License
laws.subtitle: AS 16.05.330 — Non-residents must purchase separate licenses
laws.fullDescription: Non-residents must purchase an Alaska hunting or sport fishing license before taking game or fish. Licenses are available online or at retailers. Non-resident annual hunting licenses cost $160; sport fishing licenses cost $145. Many species require additional tags or permits.
laws.penalty: Class A misdemeanor; fines up to $10,000 plus forfeiture of equipment and catch.
laws.exceptions: Alaska residents are exempt from non-resident fees. Subsistence fishing by rural residents has separate rules.

quiz.q: What class misdemeanor is fishing without a license in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Fishing without a license in Alaska is a Class A misdemeanor.

laws.title: Impaired Driving (DUI)
laws.subtitle: AS 28.35.030 — 0.08% BAC limit
laws.fullDescription: Alaska prohibits operating a motor vehicle with a BAC of 0.08% or higher. For commercial drivers the limit is 0.04%. For drivers under 21, any detectable alcohol (0.00%) is illegal. Alaska also prohibits driving under the influence of controlled substances.
laws.penalty: First offense: up to 1 year jail, $1,500 minimum fine, 90-day license revocation. Repeat offenses carry mandatory minimums and permanent revocation risks.
laws.exceptions: None — even prescription medications can trigger impairment charges if driving is impaired.

quiz.q: What is the minimum fine for a first DUI offense in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Alaska mandates a minimum $1,500 fine for a first DUI conviction.

laws.title: Open Container Law
laws.subtitle: AS 28.35.029 — No open alcohol in vehicles
laws.fullDescription: Alaska prohibits any open alcoholic beverage container in the passenger area of a motor vehicle on a public highway. The law applies to both the driver and passengers. Sealed containers in the trunk or a locked glove compartment are permitted.
laws.penalty: $300 fine; applicable to both driver and passengers possessing open containers.
laws.exceptions: Passengers in for-hire vehicles (limos, taxis) are exempt in some municipalities.

quiz.q: Can passengers drink alcohol in a private car in Alaska?
options: No, open containers are illegal for all
quiz.explanation: Alaska's open container law applies to both drivers and passengers.

laws.title: Recreational Cannabis
laws.subtitle: AS 17.38 — Legal for adults 21+
laws.fullDescription: Alaska legalized recreational cannabis in 2014 (Ballot Measure 2). Adults 21+ may possess up to 1 ounce of cannabis, 6 plants (3 mature), and concentrates in public. Consumption in public places is prohibited. Licensed retail stores operate statewide. Cannabis cannot be taken out of state.
laws.penalty: Public consumption: $100 fine. Possession over legal limits: misdemeanor or felony depending on amount.
laws.exceptions: Medical patients registered with the state may possess larger quantities.

quiz.q: How much recreational cannabis may an adult possess in public in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Alaska allows adults 21+ to possess up to 1 ounce (28g) of cannabis in public.

laws.title: Constitutional Carry
laws.subtitle: AS 11.61.220 — Permitless carry for eligible Alaskans
laws.fullDescription: Alaska is a constitutional carry state — residents and non-residents 21+ may carry a concealed handgun without a permit, provided they are legally allowed to possess a firearm. Alaska still offers optional carry permits for reciprocity purposes with other states.
laws.penalty: Carrying while prohibited (felony record, etc.): class A misdemeanor or felony depending on circumstances.
laws.exceptions: Firearms prohibited in schools, courts, government buildings, and private property posting no-gun signs.

quiz.q: Does Alaska require a permit to carry a concealed handgun?
options: No, it is a constitutional carry state
quiz.explanation: Alaska is a constitutional carry state — no permit required for eligible adults 21+.

laws.title: Background Check Requirements
laws.subtitle: AS 11.61.200 — Federal NICS checks at licensed dealers
laws.fullDescription: All firearm purchases from federally licensed dealers in Alaska require a federal background check through NICS. Alaska does not require background checks for private party sales. Prohibited persons include convicted felons, domestic violence offenders, and those involuntarily committed to psychiatric facilities.
laws.penalty: Straw purchases or transfers to prohibited persons: federal felony up to 10 years.
laws.exceptions: Transfers between immediate family members are exempt from dealer background check requirements.

quiz.q: Does Alaska require background checks for private gun sales?
options: No, only licensed dealer sales require NICS
quiz.explanation: Alaska only requires NICS background checks for sales through licensed dealers, not private sales.

laws.title: Castle Doctrine
laws.subtitle: AS 11.81.335 — Use of force in defense of premises
laws.fullDescription: Alaska law allows the use of deadly force in defense of one's home against intruders without a duty to retreat. The Castle Doctrine applies when a person reasonably believes deadly force is necessary to prevent death, serious injury, or a forcible felony inside their dwelling.
laws.penalty: N/A — this law provides a defense against criminal charges for justified use of force.
laws.exceptions: Force is not justified if the intruder is a co-resident or if the defender is engaged in criminal activity.

quiz.q: Does Alaska have a duty to retreat before using force in your home?
options: Only if the intruder is unarmed
quiz.explanation: Alaska's Castle Doctrine eliminates any duty to retreat when defending your home.

laws.title: Minimum Wage
laws.subtitle: AS 23.10.065 — Alaska minimum wage
laws.fullDescription: Alaska's minimum wage is $11.73/hour (2024), and adjusts annually with inflation per a voter-passed initiative. It exceeds the federal minimum of $7.25/hour. Tipped employees must also receive full minimum wage — tips are separate.
laws.penalty: Employers violating minimum wage laws may be liable for back wages, double damages, and attorney fees.
laws.exceptions: Certain agricultural and domestic workers may have different rates.

quiz.q: Are tipped workers in Alaska guaranteed the full minimum wage?
options: Yes, full minimum wage plus tips
Only if tips don't reach minimum wage
quiz.explanation: Alaska requires tipped workers to receive the full minimum wage; tips are additional.

laws.title: At-Will Employment
laws.subtitle: AS 23.10 — Employment at will in Alaska
laws.fullDescription: Alaska follows the at-will employment doctrine, meaning employers may terminate employees for any reason not prohibited by law, and employees may quit at any time. Alaska recognizes a public policy exception and an implied contract exception to at-will employment.
laws.penalty: N/A — at-will employment is the default standard.
laws.exceptions: Termination for illegal reasons (discrimination, retaliation for whistleblowing) is prohibited.

quiz.q: Can an Alaska employer fire an employee without giving a reason?
quiz.explanation: Alaska is an at-will employment state — employers generally may terminate without stated cause.

laws.title: Right-to-Work Law
laws.subtitle: AS 23.40.225 — Alaska is NOT a right-to-work state
laws.fullDescription: Alaska is NOT a right-to-work state. Union security agreements are permitted, meaning collective bargaining agreements can require employees in a unionized workplace to pay union dues or fees as a condition of employment. Alaska has one of the highest rates of union membership in the US.
laws.penalty: N/A — this law defines labor relations rules.
laws.exceptions: Federal employees and some other categories are governed by federal labor law.

quiz.q: Is Alaska a right-to-work state?
quiz.explanation: Alaska is NOT a right-to-work state — union security agreements are permitted.

laws.title: Non-Compete Agreements
laws.subtitle: AS 23.10 — Limited enforceability
laws.fullDescription: Alaska courts enforce non-compete agreements only if they are reasonable in scope, duration, and geographic area. Courts conduct a fact-specific analysis and will strike down overly broad agreements. Agreements up to 2 years and limited geographic scope are most likely to be upheld in Alaska.
laws.penalty: Unenforceable non-competes may be voided by a court; employers may seek injunctions for valid agreements.
laws.exceptions: Non-competes protecting legitimate trade secrets are most favored by courts.

quiz.q: Are non-compete agreements automatically enforceable in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Alaska courts enforce non-competes only if they are reasonable in scope, duration, and geography.

laws.title: Paid Sick Leave
laws.subtitle: AS 23.10.450 — Paid sick leave mandate (2024)
laws.fullDescription: Alaska voters passed Ballot Measure 1 in November 2024, requiring employers to provide paid sick leave to employees. Employees earn 1 hour of paid sick leave for every 30 hours worked. Small businesses (under 15 employees) must provide at least 3 days; larger employers must provide at least 5 days. Effective July 1, 2025.
laws.penalty: Employers violating the paid sick leave law face fines and back-pay liability.
laws.exceptions: Independent contractors are not covered. Seasonal employees have modified rules.

quiz.q: How much paid sick leave does an employee earn per 30 hours worked in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Alaska's 2024 paid sick leave law requires 1 hour earned per 30 hours worked.

laws.title: Unemployment Insurance
laws.subtitle: AS 23.20 — Alaska unemployment benefits
laws.fullDescription: Alaska's unemployment insurance provides benefits to workers who lose jobs through no fault of their own. Weekly benefits are up to $370/week for 26 weeks. Workers must have earned at least $2,500 in the base period. Alaska's remote/frontier nature leads to some of the highest claim rates in the US.
laws.penalty: Filing fraudulent unemployment claims: repayment of all benefits plus 50% penalty and possible criminal charges.
laws.exceptions: Seasonal workers, self-employed individuals, and independent contractors are generally ineligible.

quiz.q: What is the maximum weekly unemployment benefit in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Alaska's maximum weekly unemployment benefit is $370.

laws.title: Workers' Compensation
laws.subtitle: AS 23.30 — Mandatory workers' comp coverage
laws.fullDescription: Alaska requires employers with one or more employees to carry workers' compensation insurance. It covers medical expenses and lost wages for job-related injuries or illnesses. Alaska's remote work environments and resource-extraction industries make workers' comp particularly important.
laws.penalty: Employers without coverage: up to $1,000/day fine, personal liability for all claims, and stop-work orders.
laws.exceptions: Sole proprietors with no employees and some domestic workers may be exempt.

quiz.q: How many employees must an Alaska business have before workers' comp is required?
quiz.explanation: Alaska requires workers' compensation for employers with 1 or more employees.

laws.title: Independent Contractor Classification
laws.subtitle: AS 23.20.525 — ABC test for worker classification
laws.fullDescription: Alaska uses the ABC test to determine if a worker is an employee or independent contractor for unemployment insurance purposes. A worker is presumed an employee unless: (A) they work free from employer control; (B) the service is outside the employer's usual business; and (C) the worker is customarily engaged in an independent trade.
laws.penalty: Misclassifying employees as contractors: back taxes, penalties, and retroactive benefits liability.
laws.exceptions: Certain licensed professionals (attorneys, accountants) may have different classification standards.

quiz.q: What test does Alaska use for worker classification for unemployment purposes?
quiz.explanation: Alaska applies the ABC test to determine employee vs. independent contractor status.

laws.title: Child Labor Laws
laws.subtitle: AS 23.10.330 — Restrictions on youth employment
laws.fullDescription: Alaska restricts employment of minors under 18. Children under 14 may only work in limited circumstances (family businesses, agriculture, entertainment with permits). Ages 14–15 may work limited hours; ages 16–17 have fewer restrictions. All minors under 18 need work permits for most jobs.
laws.penalty: Employers violating child labor laws: civil fines up to $10,000 per violation and possible criminal charges.
laws.exceptions: Agriculture on family-owned farms and certain entertainment productions have exemptions.

quiz.q: What age do most minors need a work permit in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Alaska requires work permits for most minors under age 18.

laws.title: Equal Pay Act
laws.subtitle: AS 18.80.220 — Equal pay for equal work
laws.fullDescription: Alaska prohibits pay discrimination based on sex for substantially equal work. The Alaska Human Rights Commission enforces equal pay laws. Employers must justify pay differences based on seniority, merit, production, or factors other than sex.
laws.penalty: Back pay, compensatory damages, and attorney fees for violations.
laws.exceptions: Pay differences justified by seniority systems, merit systems, or factors unrelated to sex are permitted.

quiz.q: Which agency enforces equal pay laws in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: The Alaska Human Rights Commission enforces equal pay and anti-discrimination laws.

laws.title: Anti-Discrimination in Employment
laws.subtitle: AS 18.80.220 — Protected classes in Alaska
laws.fullDescription: Alaska prohibits employment discrimination based on race, religion, color, national origin, sex, age (40+), physical or mental disability, marital status, changes in marital status, pregnancy, or parenthood. Sexual orientation and gender identity are also protected under state law and executive order. Employers with 1+ employees are covered.
laws.penalty: Compensatory damages, back pay, reinstatement, and attorney fees.
laws.exceptions: Religious organizations may have exemptions for certain positions.

quiz.q: How many employees must an Alaska employer have before anti-discrimination laws apply?
quiz.explanation: Alaska's anti-discrimination law applies to employers with 1 or more employees.

laws.title: Landlord Entry Notice
laws.subtitle: AS 34.03.140 — 24-hour notice required
laws.fullDescription: Alaskan landlords must give tenants at least 24 hours written notice before entering a rental unit for non-emergency purposes such as repairs, inspections, or showings. The entry must be at a reasonable time. Emergency entry to prevent imminent harm is allowed without notice.
laws.penalty: Unlawful entry may entitle tenant to damages, lease termination, or an injunction.
laws.exceptions: Tenant abandonment or emergencies (fire, water leak, etc.) allow immediate entry.

quiz.q: How much notice must Alaska landlords give before entering a rental unit?
quiz.explanation: Alaska landlords must provide at least 24 hours written notice before non-emergency entry.

laws.title: Security Deposit Rules
laws.subtitle: AS 34.03.070 — Two-month maximum deposit
laws.fullDescription: Alaska landlords may not charge a security deposit exceeding two months' rent. Deposits must be returned within 14 days of lease termination (or 30 days if both parties agree). Landlords must provide an itemized statement of any deductions. Interest on deposits is not required.
laws.penalty: Landlord may forfeit right to deduct and must return full deposit plus damages up to twice the deposit.
laws.exceptions: Pet deposits may be charged separately in some cases.

quiz.q: How many days does an Alaska landlord have to return a security deposit?
quiz.explanation: Alaska landlords have 14 days to return security deposits (or 30 days with tenant agreement).

laws.title: Rent Control
laws.subtitle: AS 29.35.010 — No statewide rent control
laws.fullDescription: Alaska has no statewide rent control or rent stabilization law. Landlords may increase rent at the end of a lease term or with proper notice during a month-to-month tenancy (30 days). The Anchorage Assembly and other municipalities also cannot pass rent control under Alaska law.
laws.penalty: N/A — rent control does not exist in Alaska.
laws.exceptions: Federally subsidized housing programs have separate rent rules.

quiz.q: Can Alaska municipalities pass rent control laws?
quiz.explanation: Alaska law prohibits municipalities from enacting rent control.

laws.title: Eviction Process
laws.subtitle: AS 34.03.220 — Notice and court process required
laws.fullDescription: Alaska landlords must provide proper written notice before filing for eviction: 7 days for nonpayment of rent, 10 days for lease violations, and 30 days for no-cause termination in month-to-month tenancies. After notice expires, landlords must file in court; self-help eviction (changing locks, removing belongings) is illegal.
laws.penalty: Self-help eviction: tenant may recover actual damages, attorney fees, and up to 3 months' rent.
laws.exceptions: Emergency situations involving imminent danger may allow expedited proceedings.

quiz.q: How many days notice must Alaska landlords give for non-payment of rent before eviction?
quiz.explanation: Alaska requires 7 days written notice for non-payment of rent before starting eviction proceedings.

laws.title: Short-Term Rental Regulations
laws.subtitle: Local municipal codes — Varies by city
laws.fullDescription: Short-term rental (STR) regulations in Alaska vary by municipality. Anchorage requires STR hosts to obtain a business license and register with the municipality. Some boroughs have minimal regulation. Hosts must comply with health, safety, and tax collection requirements including local bed taxes.
laws.penalty: Operating without required licenses: fines, closure orders, and back tax liability.
laws.exceptions: Owner-occupied properties renting a single room may have reduced requirements in some municipalities.

quiz.q: Does Anchorage require short-term rental hosts to have a business license?
quiz.explanation: Anchorage requires short-term rental hosts to obtain a business license and register with the municipality.

laws.title: Property Tax
laws.subtitle: Local borough codes — No state property tax
laws.fullDescription: Alaska has no statewide property tax. Property taxes are levied by municipalities and boroughs. Rates vary widely — Anchorage has a rate of about 13.11 mills. Many rural areas of Alaska in the Unorganized Borough have no property tax at all. The senior citizen exemption applies to the first $150,000 of assessed value.
laws.penalty: Delinquent property taxes accrue interest and may result in a tax lien or foreclosure.
laws.exceptions: Senior citizens (65+) and disabled veterans receive significant exemptions.

quiz.q: Does Alaska have a statewide property tax?
options: Yes, but only on commercial property
quiz.explanation: Alaska has no statewide property tax; taxes are set by local municipalities and boroughs.

laws.title: Homestead Exemption
laws.subtitle: AS 09.38.010 — $72,900 homestead exemption
laws.fullDescription: Alaska provides a homestead exemption that protects up to $72,900 of equity in a primary residence from creditor claims in bankruptcy or civil judgments. This exemption is automatic and does not need to be declared in court. It does not reduce property tax assessments.
laws.penalty: N/A — this is a protection for homeowners, not a penalty provision.
laws.exceptions: Does not protect against tax liens, mortgage foreclosures, or mechanic's liens.

quiz.q: What is Alaska's homestead exemption amount for bankruptcy protection?
quiz.explanation: Alaska's homestead exemption protects up to $72,900 of home equity from creditors.

laws.title: State Income Tax
laws.subtitle: AS 43 — No state income tax in Alaska
laws.fullDescription: Alaska has no individual state income tax — one of only nine states with this distinction. Additionally, Alaska residents receive an annual Permanent Fund Dividend (PFD) paid from oil revenues, ranging from $1,000 to over $3,000 per year. Alaska also has no state sales tax, though municipalities may levy local sales taxes.
laws.penalty: N/A — there is no state income tax to violate.
laws.exceptions: Federal income taxes still apply to all Alaska residents.

quiz.q: Does Alaska have a state income tax?
quiz.explanation: Alaska has no state income tax and is one of only 9 states without one.

laws.title: Sales Tax
laws.subtitle: No statewide sales tax — local taxes vary
laws.fullDescription: Alaska has no statewide sales tax — one of only five states without one. However, many municipalities impose local sales taxes ranging from 1% to 7.5%. Juneau has a 5% sales tax, Ketchikan 6%, and some other cities have varying rates. Always check local rates when making purchases.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion on local sales taxes: civil penalties and possible criminal charges at the local level.
laws.exceptions: Some municipalities exempt groceries, prescription drugs, or other necessities from local sales tax.

quiz.q: Does Alaska have a statewide sales tax?
options: No, but cities may have local taxes
quiz.explanation: Alaska has no statewide sales tax, but municipalities may impose their own local sales taxes.

laws.title: Estate & Inheritance Tax
laws.subtitle: AS 43 — No state estate or inheritance tax
laws.fullDescription: Alaska has no state estate tax or inheritance tax. Estates are only subject to federal estate tax, which applies to estates exceeding the federal exemption threshold (over $13 million as of 2024). Alaska previously repealed its estate tax in 2005.
laws.penalty: N/A — no state-level estate tax exists.
laws.exceptions: Federal estate tax still applies to very large estates.

quiz.q: Does Alaska have a state estate tax?
quiz.explanation: Alaska has no state estate tax; only federal estate tax may apply.

laws.title: Smoke-Free Workplace Law
laws.subtitle: AS 18.35.301 — Clean Indoor Air Act
laws.fullDescription: Alaska's Clean Indoor Air Act prohibits smoking in most enclosed workplaces, restaurants, bars, and public places. E-cigarettes and vaping products are also restricted in many indoor spaces. Local municipalities may have stricter rules. Employers must post no-smoking signs and maintain smoke-free environments.
laws.penalty: Violation: $50–$300 fine per incident for individuals; employers may face larger fines for non-compliance.
laws.exceptions: Some private clubs and tribal facilities may have limited exemptions.

quiz.q: Are vaping and e-cigarettes restricted indoors in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Alaska extends its indoor smoke-free rules to e-cigarettes and vaping in many settings.

laws.title: Helmet Laws
laws.subtitle: AS 28.35.240 — Motorcycle helmets required for under 18
laws.fullDescription: Alaska requires helmets for motorcycle operators and passengers under 18 years of age. Adults 18 and older may ride without helmets. All motorcycle riders must wear eye protection unless the bike has a windshield. Bicycle helmets are not mandated by state law, though some municipalities may require them for minors.
laws.penalty: Violation of motorcycle helmet law: $50–$200 fine.
laws.exceptions: Adults 18+ may legally ride without helmets in Alaska.

quiz.q: Must adults over 18 wear a motorcycle helmet in Alaska?
options: No, helmets are only required under 18
quiz.explanation: Alaska only requires motorcycle helmets for riders under 18; adults may ride helmet-free.

laws.title: Seatbelt Law
laws.subtitle: AS 28.05.095 — Mandatory seatbelts
laws.fullDescription: Alaska requires all front-seat occupants to wear seatbelts. Passengers under 16 in any seating position must be buckled. Children under 4 or under 40 lbs must be in a child safety seat. Violations are primary offenses — police can pull over vehicles solely for seatbelt non-compliance.
laws.penalty: $15 fine for adult front-seat violation; higher fines for child restraint violations.
laws.exceptions: Some commercial truck drivers and passengers in medical emergencies may have limited exemptions.

quiz.q: What is the fine for an adult not wearing a seatbelt in the front seat in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Alaska's front-seat seatbelt violation fine is $15 for adults.

laws.title: Speed Limits
laws.subtitle: AS 28.40.100 — Statutory speed limits
laws.fullDescription: Alaska's default speed limits: 55 mph on rural two-lane highways, 65–70 mph on divided highways where posted, 20 mph in school zones, 25 mph in residential areas, and 55 mph on the open road. Alaska also has strict laws against 'speed competition' (street racing), which is a criminal offense.
laws.penalty: Speeding fines start at $50 and increase with severity. Racing is a class A misdemeanor with potential jail.
laws.exceptions: Emergency vehicles are exempt from speed limits when responding.

quiz.q: What is the default speed limit in Alaska residential areas?
quiz.explanation: Alaska's default residential speed limit is 25 mph unless otherwise posted.

laws.title: Texting While Driving
laws.subtitle: AS 28.35.161 — Handheld device ban while driving
laws.fullDescription: Alaska bans all handheld use of electronic devices while driving, including texting, emailing, browsing, and calling. Drivers must use hands-free options. This is a primary offense and Alaska has one of the highest distracted driving fines in the US.
laws.penalty: First offense: $500; second offense: $1,000; third+ offense: $10,000.
laws.exceptions: Emergency calls to 911 are permitted.

quiz.q: What is the fine for a third handheld device offense while driving in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Alaska's third-offense fine for using a handheld device while driving is $10,000 — one of the highest in the US.

laws.title: DUI Checkpoint Legality
laws.subtitle: AS 28.35 — Sobriety checkpoints permitted
laws.fullDescription: DUI sobriety checkpoints are legal in Alaska under both state law and the Fourth Amendment balancing test. Law enforcement agencies must follow established procedures including public notice, neutral vehicle selection criteria, and brief stops. Alaska Supreme Court has upheld checkpoint programs.
laws.penalty: N/A — this law defines when checkpoints are legal; DUI penalties apply to impaired drivers found.
laws.exceptions: Checkpoints may not be set up to conduct general vehicle inspections unrelated to sobriety.

quiz.q: Are DUI sobriety checkpoints legal in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: DUI sobriety checkpoints are legal in Alaska when conducted with proper procedures.

laws.title: Move Over Law
laws.subtitle: AS 28.35.185 — Slow or move over for emergency vehicles
laws.fullDescription: Alaska's Move Over Law requires drivers to change lanes or slow down when passing stopped emergency vehicles (police, fire, ambulance), tow trucks, or road maintenance vehicles with flashing lights on the roadway or shoulder. If a lane change is not possible, reduce speed significantly.
laws.penalty: Violation: $300 fine; if the violation results in injury or death, criminal charges may apply.
laws.exceptions: Move over requirement applies only when it is safe to do so without creating a greater hazard.

quiz.q: Does Alaska's Move Over Law apply to tow trucks?
quiz.explanation: Alaska's Move Over Law covers police, fire, ambulance, tow trucks, and road maintenance vehicles.

laws.title: Age of Majority
laws.subtitle: AS 25.20.010 — Age 18 is legal adulthood
laws.fullDescription: In Alaska, the age of majority is 18. At 18, Alaskans gain the right to vote, enter contracts, sue and be sued, marry without parental consent, and make their own medical decisions. Minors under 18 may be emancipated by court order and gain adult legal status.
laws.penalty: N/A — this defines civil rights, not criminal penalties.
laws.exceptions: Some rights have higher age thresholds: alcohol (21), handgun purchase from dealers (21), cannabis (21).

quiz.q: At what age does a person reach the age of majority in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Alaska's age of majority is 18.

laws.title: Voting Rights & Restoration
laws.subtitle: AS 15.05.010 — Voter eligibility in Alaska
laws.fullDescription: Alaska residents must be US citizens, age 18+, and reside in Alaska to vote. Felons lose voting rights during incarceration and parole/probation. Voting rights are automatically restored upon completion of sentence including probation. No waiting period after restoration.
laws.penalty: Voting while ineligible (while incarcerated): class A misdemeanor.
laws.exceptions: Persons found mentally incompetent by a court lose voting rights during incapacity.

quiz.q: When are voting rights restored to a felon in Alaska?
options: Automatically after completing sentence including probation
After applying to the parole board
quiz.explanation: Alaska automatically restores voting rights when a felon completes their sentence including probation.

laws.title: Jury Duty
laws.subtitle: AS 09.20.010 — Jury service requirements
laws.fullDescription: Alaska residents who are US citizens, 18+, and registered voters may be called for jury duty. Service is mandatory unless granted a postponement or exemption. Jurors receive $12.50/day for the first 4 days, then $25/day thereafter plus mileage. Employers must allow employees to serve without firing them.
laws.penalty: Willfully ignoring a jury summons: contempt of court, up to $500 fine.
laws.exceptions: Exemptions include active military, police officers, firefighters, and those with extreme hardship.

quiz.q: What is the daily rate for Alaska jurors after the first 4 days?
quiz.explanation: Alaska jurors receive $25 per day after the first 4 days of service.

laws.title: Mandatory Reporting of Child Abuse
laws.subtitle: AS 47.17.020 — All Alaskans are mandatory reporters
laws.fullDescription: Alaska is one of relatively few states where all adults (not just certain professionals) are mandatory reporters of suspected child abuse or neglect. Suspected abuse must be reported to the Office of Children's Services (OCS) or law enforcement immediately. Reports made in good faith are protected from liability.
laws.penalty: Failure to report known child abuse: class A misdemeanor, up to 1 year jail.
laws.exceptions: Attorney-client privilege may apply in some limited circumstances.

quiz.q: Who is a mandatory reporter of child abuse in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Alaska requires all adults to report suspected child abuse — not just certain professions.

laws.title: Age of Consent
laws.subtitle: AS 11.41.434 — Age of consent is 16
laws.fullDescription: Alaska's age of consent is 16. Sexual activity with a person under 16 by someone 3 or more years older is statutory sexual abuse. Alaska also has close-in-age exemptions (Romeo and Juliet provisions) and has strict laws against online solicitation of minors. Sex offenders must register with the Alaska Sex Offender Registry.
laws.penalty: Sexual abuse of a minor: class B or A felony depending on circumstances; mandatory sex offender registration.
laws.exceptions: Romeo and Juliet provision for consensual activity between minors of similar age.

quiz.q: What is Alaska's age of consent?
quiz.explanation: Alaska's age of consent is 16.

laws.title: Emancipation of Minors
laws.subtitle: AS 09.55.590 — Court-ordered emancipation
laws.fullDescription: Alaska allows minors aged 16 and 17 to petition the court for emancipation, which grants them adult legal status. The court considers whether emancipation is in the minor's best interests, whether the minor can support themselves financially, and whether they are mature enough for independent living.
laws.penalty: N/A — emancipation is a civil court process, not a criminal matter.
laws.exceptions: Emancipation does not override laws setting minimum ages for alcohol, cannabis, or voting.

quiz.q: At what minimum age can a minor petition for emancipation in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Alaska allows minors aged 16+ to petition for court-ordered emancipation.

laws.title: Curfew Laws
laws.subtitle: Local municipal ordinances — varies by city
laws.fullDescription: Alaska has no statewide youth curfew law. Individual municipalities may enact their own curfews. Anchorage has a curfew for minors under 16 between midnight and 5 a.m. Juneau and other cities have similar provisions. Parents may be liable if their minor repeatedly violates curfew.
laws.penalty: Curfew violation: minor may be taken into custody and released to parents; parents may face fines.
laws.exceptions: Minors with parental supervision, employment, or traveling to/from school activities are typically exempt.

quiz.q: Does Alaska have a statewide youth curfew law?
quiz.explanation: Alaska has no statewide curfew; municipalities set their own rules.

laws.title: Corporal Punishment in Schools
laws.subtitle: AS 14.33.120 — Corporal punishment prohibited in public schools
laws.fullDescription: Alaska prohibits corporal punishment (physical discipline) in all public schools. Private schools are not explicitly covered by state law, but most follow the same policy. Physical restraint of students is only allowed to prevent imminent harm and must be reported.
laws.penalty: Educators using corporal punishment in public schools face administrative discipline and potential criminal charges.
laws.exceptions: Physical restraint (not punishment) is permitted only when necessary to prevent imminent harm.

quiz.q: Is corporal punishment allowed in Alaska public schools?
options: No — it is prohibited in public schools
quiz.explanation: Alaska prohibits corporal punishment in all public schools.

laws.title: Homeschooling Regulations
laws.subtitle: AS 14.30.010 — Homeschooling permitted
laws.fullDescription: Alaska allows homeschooling and offers multiple options: home study with state correspondence programs, charter school enrollment, or independent homeschooling. Families choosing fully independent homeschooling must provide a basic education in required subjects. Alaska is unique in offering state-funded correspondence study programs to home-schoolers.
laws.penalty: Failure to provide basic education: child may be placed in compulsory public schooling.
laws.exceptions: Native Alaskan villages with limited school access have special provisions.

quiz.q: Does Alaska offer state-funded correspondence programs for home-schoolers?
quiz.explanation: Alaska uniquely offers state-funded correspondence study programs for homeschooled students.

laws.title: School Vaccination Requirements
laws.subtitle: 7 AAC 27 — Required vaccinations for school entry
laws.fullDescription: Alaska requires students entering school to be vaccinated against diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, measles, mumps, rubella, varicella, and hepatitis B. Parents may request medical or non-medical (religious/philosophical) exemptions. Non-vaccinated students may be excluded during disease outbreaks.
laws.penalty: Unvaccinated students without exemptions may be excluded from school.
laws.exceptions: Medical, religious, and philosophical exemptions are available upon written request.

quiz.q: Can Alaska parents claim a philosophical exemption from school vaccinations?
options: Yes — medical and non-medical exemptions available
quiz.explanation: Alaska allows medical and non-medical (religious/philosophical) vaccination exemptions.

laws.title: Abortion Laws
laws.subtitle: AS 18.16 — Abortion legal in Alaska
laws.fullDescription: Abortion is legal in Alaska throughout pregnancy. The Alaska Supreme Court has ruled that the right to privacy in the Alaska Constitution includes the right to an abortion. There is no gestational limit under state law. Minors may obtain abortions without parental consent, though notification requirements have been debated.
laws.penalty: N/A — abortion is legal with no criminal penalty for patients or providers under Alaska law.
laws.exceptions: State law requires abortions to be performed by licensed medical professionals.

quiz.q: Does Alaska's constitution protect the right to abortion?
options: Yes — under the right to privacy
quiz.explanation: The Alaska Supreme Court has ruled the state constitutional right to privacy protects abortion access.

laws.title: Death Penalty
laws.subtitle: AS 12.55 — Alaska abolished death penalty in 1957
laws.fullDescription: Alaska abolished the death penalty in 1957, before statehood in 1959. Alaska remains one of the few US states to never have had the death penalty as a state. The maximum punishment for murder in Alaska is 99 years in prison (or life without parole for aggravated first-degree murder).
laws.penalty: Maximum penalty for first-degree murder: 99 years or life without parole.
laws.exceptions: Federal crimes committed in Alaska may carry the federal death penalty.

quiz.q: When did Alaska abolish the death penalty?
quiz.explanation: Alaska abolished the death penalty in 1957, two years before statehood.

laws.title: Medical Aid in Dying
laws.subtitle: No law — MAID not legal in Alaska
laws.fullDescription: Medical aid in dying (physician-assisted suicide) is not legal in Alaska. Bills have been introduced in the Alaska legislature but have not passed. Terminally ill patients do not have a legal right to a prescription for life-ending medication. Palliative care and hospice services are available statewide.
laws.penalty: Assisting a suicide: class B felony under AS 11.41.120.
laws.exceptions: Withdrawal of life support and palliative sedation are legal with patient consent.

quiz.q: Is medical aid in dying (assisted suicide) legal in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Medical aid in dying is not legal in Alaska — assisting a suicide is a class B felony.

laws.title: Drug Penalties (Non-Cannabis)
laws.subtitle: AS 11.71 — Controlled Substances Act
laws.fullDescription: Alaska categorizes controlled substances in schedules IA through VIA. Possession of heroin, meth, cocaine, or other serious drugs is a class C felony. Delivery or manufacture of schedule IA substances is a class A felony carrying up to 99 years. Alaska has drug treatment diversion programs for first-time offenders.
laws.penalty: Possession of hard drugs: class C felony, up to 5 years. Distribution/manufacture of class IA: up to 99 years.
laws.exceptions: Prescribed medications are exempt when used as directed. Medical cannabis is separately regulated.

quiz.q: What class of felony is simple possession of heroin in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Possession of heroin and other schedule IA drugs in Alaska is a class C felony.

laws.title: Asset Forfeiture
laws.subtitle: AS 17.30.112 — Civil asset forfeiture in Alaska
laws.fullDescription: Alaska allows civil asset forfeiture for property connected to drug crimes and certain other felonies. Law enforcement may seize and seek to keep property without a criminal conviction, though Alaska has stronger protections than many states. The owner may contest the forfeiture in court, and the burden shifts to the state to prove the connection to crime.
laws.penalty: N/A — forfeiture is an action against property, not a criminal penalty.
laws.exceptions: Innocent owner defense: property returned if owner proves no knowledge of criminal use.

quiz.q: Can Alaska seize assets without a criminal conviction?
quiz.explanation: Alaska permits civil asset forfeiture; property can be seized without a criminal conviction.

laws.title: Expungement & Record Sealing
laws.subtitle: AS 12.62.180 — Limited expungement in Alaska
laws.fullDescription: Alaska has limited expungement options. Juvenile records may be sealed. Adult records for some first-time, low-level offenses may be set aside (vacated) after completing probation or sentence. Full expungement (complete destruction of records) is rare and requires specific circumstances. A 'set aside' removes some consequences but the record still exists.
laws.penalty: N/A — this is a post-conviction relief process.
laws.exceptions: Serious felonies, sex offenses, and domestic violence convictions generally cannot be set aside or expunged.

quiz.q: Can all adult criminal convictions be expunged in Alaska?
options: No — expungement is limited in Alaska
quiz.explanation: Alaska has very limited expungement; most adult records can only be 'set aside,' not fully expunged.

laws.title: Solitary Confinement
laws.subtitle: AS 33.30 — DOC regulations
laws.fullDescription: Alaska's Department of Corrections has policies limiting solitary confinement (restricted housing). Reforms in recent years have reduced its use for vulnerable populations. Alaska prisons must provide minimum out-of-cell time and mental health checks for those in restricted housing. Advocacy groups continue to push for further reforms.
laws.penalty: N/A — this governs prison administration policy.
laws.exceptions: Extremely dangerous or disruptive inmates may be held in restricted housing for longer periods.

quiz.q: Has Alaska reformed its use of solitary confinement in recent years?
options: Yes, reduced use for vulnerable populations
quiz.explanation: Alaska has implemented reforms reducing solitary confinement, especially for vulnerable populations.

laws.title: Private Prison Use
laws.subtitle: AS 33.30 — No private prisons in Alaska
laws.fullDescription: Alaska does not use privately operated prisons for its general inmate population. The Alaska Department of Corrections operates all state correctional facilities. Alaska has, however, contracted with out-of-state facilities to house some prisoners due to overcrowding, which has raised advocacy concerns.
laws.penalty: N/A — this is a policy/legislative issue, not a criminal law.
laws.exceptions: Some community correctional facilities and halfway houses are privately operated under state contracts.

quiz.q: Does Alaska use privately operated prisons?
quiz.explanation: Alaska does not use private prisons — all state correctional facilities are government-operated.

laws.title: Body Camera Requirements
laws.subtitle: DPS Policy — Encouraged but not mandated statewide
laws.fullDescription: Alaska has no statewide law mandating body cameras for law enforcement officers. The Alaska Department of Public Safety (state troopers) uses body cameras by policy. Anchorage Police and other local departments have their own body camera programs. Footage retention policies vary by agency.
laws.penalty: N/A — no statewide mandate exists; violations handled by department policy.
laws.exceptions: Individual agencies set their own body camera and footage retention policies.

quiz.q: Does Alaska have a statewide law requiring police body cameras?
options: No — state troopers use them by policy, not law
quiz.explanation: Alaska has no statewide body camera mandate; departments set their own policies.

laws.title: Police Use of Force
laws.subtitle: AS 11.81.370 — Force justified in law enforcement
laws.fullDescription: Alaska law justifies law enforcement use of force to make lawful arrests or prevent escape of dangerous persons. Deadly force is only justified when the officer reasonably believes it necessary to prevent death or serious injury. The Alaska Supreme Court has emphasized proportionality. Alaska troopers have specific de-escalation training requirements.
laws.penalty: Unjustified use of force: potential criminal charges against officers; civil liability.
laws.exceptions: Force is always subject to the reasonableness standard and proportionality principles.

quiz.q: When can Alaska law enforcement use deadly force?
options: When reasonably necessary to prevent death or serious injury
quiz.explanation: Alaska officers may only use deadly force when reasonably necessary to prevent death or serious physical injury.

laws.title: Extreme Risk Protection Orders (ERPO)
laws.subtitle: No ERPO law in Alaska
laws.fullDescription: Alaska does not have an Extreme Risk Protection Order (Red Flag) law. Attempts to pass ERPO legislation have not succeeded in the Alaska Legislature. Law enforcement can still petition for involuntary psychiatric evaluation if someone poses an imminent threat, which may result in temporary firearm restrictions.
laws.penalty: N/A — no ERPO law exists.
laws.exceptions: Existing domestic violence protective orders may include firearm surrender requirements.

quiz.q: Does Alaska have a Red Flag (ERPO) law?
quiz.explanation: Alaska does not have an Extreme Risk Protection Order (Red Flag) law.

laws.title: Hate Crime Laws
laws.subtitle: AS 12.55.155 — Bias-motivated crime enhancements
laws.fullDescription: Alaska law provides sentencing enhancements for crimes motivated by the victim's race, religion, sex, color, national origin, or ancestry. The enhancement adds to the sentence of the underlying crime. Physical assault motivated by bias can result in significantly longer sentences.
laws.penalty: Bias motivation adds 0.5–2 years to standard sentencing guidelines depending on the underlying offense.
laws.exceptions: Speech expressing bias, without accompanying criminal conduct, is constitutionally protected.

quiz.q: How does Alaska punish hate crimes?
options: Sentencing enhancements to the underlying crime
quiz.explanation: Alaska addresses hate crimes through sentencing enhancements to the underlying criminal charge.

laws.title: Domestic Violence Protections
laws.subtitle: AS 18.66 — Domestic Violence Prevention Act
laws.fullDescription: Alaska has high rates of domestic violence — among the highest in the US. The Domestic Violence Prevention Act provides protective orders, mandatory arrest policies for probable cause DV, and victim advocacy programs. Alaska's Safe Surrenders program protects firearms from abusers. Violation of a DV protective order is a criminal offense.
laws.penalty: Violation of a DV protective order: class A misdemeanor, up to 1 year jail.
laws.exceptions: Mutual protective orders may be issued in some circumstances.

quiz.q: Does Alaska have mandatory arrest policies for domestic violence?
options: Yes — officers must arrest on probable cause
quiz.explanation: Alaska has mandatory arrest policies for domestic violence when officers have probable cause.

laws.title: Stalking & Cyberstalking
laws.subtitle: AS 11.41.270 — Stalking first and second degree
laws.fullDescription: Alaska prohibits stalking, defined as repeated non-consensual contact that would cause a reasonable person substantial distress. First-degree stalking (involving a weapon, violating a protective order, or when the victim is under 16) is a class C felony. Second-degree stalking is a class A misdemeanor. Cyberstalking through electronic means is covered.
laws.penalty: First-degree stalking: class C felony, up to 5 years. Second-degree: class A misdemeanor, up to 1 year.
laws.exceptions: Lawful investigations by law enforcement are not considered stalking.

quiz.q: What degree of felony is stalking when the victim is under 16 in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Stalking a victim under 16 in Alaska is first-degree stalking, a class C felony.

laws.title: Data Privacy Law
laws.subtitle: No comprehensive state privacy law in Alaska yet
laws.fullDescription: Alaska does not yet have a comprehensive consumer data privacy law comparable to California's CCPA. Limited protections exist under the Alaska Personal Information Protection Act (APIPA) for security breach notification. Businesses holding personal data of Alaskans must notify residents of security breaches within a reasonable time.
laws.penalty: Failure to notify of a data breach: civil fines up to $25,000 per violation.
laws.exceptions: Businesses with fewer than 10 employees have simplified notification requirements.

quiz.q: Does Alaska have a comprehensive consumer data privacy law?
quiz.explanation: Alaska only has data breach notification requirements, not a comprehensive consumer privacy law.

laws.title: Social Media Age Verification
laws.subtitle: No state law — pending federal legislation
laws.fullDescription: Alaska does not have a state law requiring age verification for social media platforms. This is currently being addressed at the federal level. Schools and libraries in Alaska implement their own filtering and age-appropriate access policies under CIPA requirements for federal funding.
laws.penalty: N/A — no state law exists.
laws.exceptions: School and library internet access has federally mandated filtering requirements.

quiz.q: Does Alaska require social media platforms to verify user ages?
quiz.explanation: Alaska has no state law on social media age verification; this is a federal policy debate.

laws.title: Environmental Regulations
laws.subtitle: AS 46 — Alaska Environmental Conservation laws
laws.fullDescription: Alaska's Department of Environmental Conservation regulates air quality, water quality, and waste management. Alaska has strict protections for its pristine wilderness including the Tongass National Forest, Arctic National Wildlife Refuge (ANWR), and major salmon rivers. Oil spill prevention regulations are especially stringent following the 1989 Exxon Valdez disaster.
laws.penalty: Environmental violations: civil fines up to $25,000/day; criminal penalties for willful violations.
laws.exceptions: Some subsistence uses by Alaska Native peoples have special protections.

quiz.q: What 1989 disaster led to stricter oil spill regulations in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: The 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill in Prince William Sound led to major oil spill prevention regulation reform.

laws.title: Renewable Energy Standards
laws.subtitle: AS 42.45.045 — Renewable Energy Grant Fund
laws.fullDescription: Alaska has a goal of 50% renewable energy by 2025 for rural communities (through the Alaska Energy Authority). The state's vast geography makes renewable energy critical — solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal projects are funded through state grants. The Renewable Energy Grant Fund supports projects across the state.
laws.penalty: N/A — this is a goal and funding program, not a mandate with penalties.
laws.exceptions: Urban utilities have different standards; the goal primarily targets rural communities.

quiz.q: What is Alaska's renewable energy goal for rural communities?
quiz.explanation: Alaska's goal is 50% renewable energy for rural communities by 2025 through the Alaska Energy Authority.

laws.title: Plastic Bag Laws
laws.subtitle: Local municipal codes — No statewide ban
laws.fullDescription: Alaska has no statewide plastic bag ban or fee. Some municipalities like Juneau have enacted local plastic bag ordinances. Most of Alaska has no bag restrictions. Environmental advocacy groups continue to push for statewide legislation given the impact of plastic on Alaska's marine ecosystems.
laws.penalty: Municipal violations vary — typically small fines for retailers not complying with local ordinances.
laws.exceptions: Bags used for meat, produce, or bulk items are often exempt from local bans.

quiz.q: Does Alaska have a statewide plastic bag ban?
options: Yes, but only for large stores
quiz.explanation: Alaska has no statewide plastic bag ban; some municipalities like Juneau have local ordinances.

laws.title: Bottle Deposit Law
laws.subtitle: AS 46.06 — No statewide bottle deposit
laws.fullDescription: Alaska does not have a statewide bottle deposit/redemption program (unlike California, Oregon, and Michigan). There have been proposals, but high logistics costs in remote areas make implementation challenging. Recycling in Alaska relies primarily on municipal curbside programs and private recyclers.
laws.penalty: N/A — no bottle deposit law exists.
laws.exceptions: Some municipalities run voluntary redemption programs.

quiz.q: Does Alaska have a bottle deposit/redemption program?
quiz.explanation: Alaska does not have a statewide bottle deposit program.

laws.title: Animal Cruelty Laws
laws.subtitle: AS 11.61.140 — Animal cruelty
laws.fullDescription: Alaska prohibits cruelty to animals, including torture, beating, poisoning, or depriving an animal of food and water. Intentional, serious cruelty is a class C felony. Neglect (misdemeanor) is the most common charge. Animal hoarding is addressed under neglect statutes. The 2020 'Provoked Dog' law addresses dog fighting.
laws.penalty: Misdemeanor cruelty: up to 1 year jail. Felony cruelty (intentional): class C felony, up to 5 years.
laws.exceptions: Hunting and fishing as permitted by license, pest control, and veterinary procedures are exempt.

quiz.q: What class of felony is intentional serious animal cruelty in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Intentional serious animal cruelty in Alaska is a class C felony.

laws.title: Exotic Pet Laws
laws.subtitle: AS 03.55.020 — Prohibited wild animal ownership
laws.fullDescription: Alaska prohibits ownership of many wild and exotic animals including wolves, bears, big cats, venomous snakes, and certain primates as pets. Animals posing a public health or safety risk are banned. A few species may be kept with a permit from the Alaska Department of Fish and Game.
laws.penalty: Unlawful possession of prohibited exotic animal: class B misdemeanor; animal may be seized and relocated.
laws.exceptions: Wildlife rehabilitators, zoos, and research institutions with proper permits may keep otherwise prohibited animals.

quiz.q: Can Alaskans keep wolves as pets?
options: No — wolves are prohibited as pets
quiz.explanation: Alaska prohibits keeping wolves and most wild animals as pets; they are dangerous to public safety.

laws.title: Fireworks Laws
laws.subtitle: AS 18.72 — Fireworks regulated by municipalities
laws.fullDescription: Alaska regulates consumer fireworks under state fire safety codes. Municipalities have the authority to impose stricter rules. In Anchorage, only 'safe and sane' fireworks are allowed; aerial fireworks are prohibited without a permit. In rural areas and the Kenai Peninsula, rules are more relaxed. Always check local ordinances.
laws.penalty: Violation of fireworks ordinances: $500–$2,000 fines plus liability for fire damage.
laws.exceptions: Licensed pyrotechnic operators may use professional grade fireworks at permitted events.

quiz.q: Are aerial fireworks generally allowed in Anchorage?
options: No — only safe and sane fireworks allowed
quiz.explanation: Anchorage prohibits aerial fireworks for consumers; only 'safe and sane' fireworks are allowed.

laws.title: Gambling Laws
laws.subtitle: AS 05.15 — Alaska gambling restrictions
laws.fullDescription: Alaska has very limited legal gambling. There are no commercial casinos, slot machines, or video poker terminals. Bingo, pull tabs, and charitable gaming are permitted. Dog mushing races (including the famous Iditarod) may involve pari-mutuel wagering. Online gambling is not regulated by the state.
laws.penalty: Promoting illegal gambling: class A misdemeanor; running an illegal gambling enterprise: class C felony.
laws.exceptions: Charitable gaming (bingo, pull tabs) for nonprofits is permitted with a license.

quiz.q: Are commercial casinos legal in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Alaska has no commercial casinos; only charitable gaming (bingo, pull tabs) is permitted.

laws.title: Bear Encounter Laws
laws.subtitle: AS 16.05 — Hunting regulations & wildlife interaction
laws.fullDescription: In Alaska, encounters with brown bears, black bears, and polar bears are common. It is legal to kill a bear in defense of life or property. However, wanton waste of the animal is prohibited — the meat must be salvaged. Feeding bears is prohibited and can result in fines. Bear-resistant containers are required in certain national parks.
laws.penalty: Wanton waste (not salvaging bear killed in defense): class A misdemeanor. Feeding bears: up to $1,000 fine.
laws.exceptions: Licensed bear hunts follow specific regulations with allocated tags and seasons.

quiz.q: If you kill a bear in self-defense in Alaska, what must you do?
options: Salvage the meat (wanton waste is illegal)
Turn in the bear to ADF&G immediately
quiz.explanation: Even if you kill a bear legally in self-defense, Alaska law requires you to salvage the meat — wanton waste is a misdemeanor.

laws.title: Snowmobile Regulations
laws.subtitle: AS 28.90 — Snowmobile/ATV operating rules
laws.fullDescription: Snowmobiles (snow machines) are a primary mode of transportation in rural Alaska. They must be registered with the state unless operated solely on private property. Operating a snow machine on public roads is prohibited except for crossing. Speed limits and safety equipment requirements apply on trails. DUI laws apply to snow machine operators.
laws.penalty: Unregistered operation on public trails: $50–$500 fine. DUI on a snow machine: same as vehicle DUI.
laws.exceptions: Use on private property does not require registration or public use rules.

quiz.q: Do Alaska DUI laws apply to snowmobile operators?
options: Yes — same penalties as vehicle DUI
quiz.explanation: Alaska DUI laws apply to snowmobile operators just as they do to motor vehicle drivers.

laws.title: Subsistence Fishing Rights
laws.subtitle: AS 16.05.940 — Subsistence priority system
laws.fullDescription: Alaska law establishes a subsistence priority system for fish and game resources, giving rural Alaskans and Alaska Natives priority access for subsistence (personal/family food) use. In years of shortage, subsistence users have priority over sport and commercial fishers. Federal and state subsistence programs overlap and sometimes conflict.
laws.penalty: Taking fish in violation of subsistence regulations: same penalties as unlicensed fishing, plus possible federal charges.
laws.exceptions: Urban residents in municipalities are generally not eligible for state subsistence preference.

quiz.q: Who has priority access to fish and game under Alaska's subsistence system?
quiz.explanation: Alaska's subsistence priority system gives rural Alaskans and Alaska Natives first access to fish and game resources.

laws.title: Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend
laws.subtitle: AS 43.23 — Annual payment to Alaska residents
laws.fullDescription: Alaska's Permanent Fund Dividend (PFD) is an annual payment to Alaska residents from investment earnings of the Alaska Permanent Fund, which is funded by oil revenues. To qualify, residents must live in Alaska for a full calendar year and intend to remain. The 2023 PFD was $1,312. The amount varies with fund performance and legislative appropriations.
laws.penalty: Fraudulently claiming the PFD: repayment plus a civil penalty up to $1,000 and possible criminal charges.
laws.exceptions: Inmates convicted of felonies are not eligible for the PFD during incarceration.

quiz.q: What fund generates money for Alaska's Permanent Fund Dividend?
quiz.explanation: The Alaska Permanent Fund is funded by oil revenues, with investment earnings distributed as annual PFD payments.

laws.title: Aerial Hunting Prohibition
laws.subtitle: AS 16.05.783 — Aerial shooting of game generally prohibited
laws.fullDescription: Alaska law prohibits hunting game animals from aircraft, landing from an aircraft and hunting the same day, or using aircraft to spot game and then hunt on foot the same day. These restrictions prevent unfair advantage over wildlife. Wolf control programs authorized by the Board of Game are a controversial exception.
laws.penalty: Aerial hunting violation: up to $10,000 fine and loss of hunting license for up to 3 years.
laws.exceptions: State-authorized wolf and predator control programs may use aerial methods. Reporting dead or wounded game from air is allowed.

quiz.q: Is it legal to land from an aircraft and immediately hunt in Alaska?
options: No — same-day airborne hunting is prohibited
quiz.explanation: Alaska prohibits landing from an aircraft and hunting on the same day — it creates an unfair advantage over wildlife.

laws.title: Winter Driving Requirements
laws.subtitle: AS 28.35 — Seasonal tire and safety rules
laws.fullDescription: Alaska does not mandate studded tires statewide, but studded tires are permitted from September 15 through May 1. Drivers are expected to have tires suitable for winter conditions. Alaska law requires headlights to be on whenever visibility is reduced. Vehicles must be cleared of snow before driving to avoid creating hazards for other drivers.
laws.penalty: Driving with unsecured snow/ice on vehicle that causes injury: up to $500 fine; causing injury raises liability.
laws.exceptions: Some vehicle categories have different seasonal tire specifications.

quiz.q: When are studded tires permitted in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Alaska allows studded tires from September 15 through May 1.

laws.title: Kratom Regulation
laws.subtitle: No statewide ban — kratom legal in Alaska
laws.fullDescription: Kratom is legal in Alaska — there is no state ban or significant regulation of the herbal supplement. Alaska is not among the states that have banned or heavily regulated kratom. Federal regulations apply to labeling and safety claims. Some municipalities may have additional restrictions.
laws.penalty: N/A — kratom is unregulated at the state level.
laws.exceptions: FDA warnings about kratom apply nationally regardless of state legality.

quiz.q: Is kratom legal in Alaska?
options: Yes — unregulated at the state level
quiz.explanation: Kratom is legal and largely unregulated in Alaska.

laws.title: Oil Spill Liability
laws.subtitle: AS 46.03.822 — Oil spill strict liability
laws.fullDescription: Alaska imposes strict liability for oil spills — responsible parties are liable for cleanup costs and damages regardless of fault, following the Exxon Valdez disaster. The Oil and Hazardous Substance Release Prevention and Response Fund provides emergency funding. Companies operating in Alaska waters must have oil spill contingency plans approved by DEC.
laws.penalty: Failure to clean up a spill: civil penalties up to $500,000/day plus full cleanup and damage costs.
laws.exceptions: Acts of God or actions of third parties may modify liability in limited circumstances.

quiz.q: Is Alaska oil spill liability fault-based or strict liability?
quiz.explanation: Alaska's oil spill law imposes strict liability — responsible parties are liable regardless of fault.

laws.title: Marine Mammal Protection
laws.subtitle: Federal MMPA + AS 16.05 — Marine mammal rules
laws.fullDescription: Marine mammals (whales, seals, sea lions, walrus, polar bears, sea otters) are protected under the federal Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA). Alaska Natives may take marine mammals for subsistence purposes and for creating handicrafts under federal exemption. Harassment of marine mammals (including whale watching at close range) is a federal offense enforced in Alaska waters.
laws.penalty: MMPA violation: up to $10,000 civil penalty; criminal violations up to $20,000 and 1 year jail.
laws.exceptions: Alaska Native subsistence harvest and handicraft use are specifically exempted under the MMPA.

quiz.q: Who may legally harvest marine mammals in Alaska for subsistence?
quiz.explanation: Only Alaska Natives may harvest marine mammals for subsistence under a federal MMPA exemption.

laws.title: Alaska Native Employment Preferences
laws.subtitle: AS 36.10.150 — Alaska hire preferences
laws.fullDescription: Alaska law provides employment preferences for Alaska residents over non-residents in certain state-funded construction and public works projects. Alaska Native hire preferences apply to some state and federal programs. Court decisions have complicated mandatory hire preferences, but voluntary preferences and targeted outreach programs remain common.
laws.penalty: N/A — this law defines preferences and outreach requirements.
laws.exceptions: Federal contractors may have different requirements under federal Indian preference laws.

quiz.q: Does Alaska law provide employment preferences for state residents on state construction projects?
quiz.explanation: Alaska law historically provided resident hire preferences for state-funded construction projects, though court challenges have modified implementation.

laws.title: Commercial Fishing Regulations
laws.subtitle: AS 16.05 — Fisheries management and licensing
laws.fullDescription: Alaska has one of the world's most valuable commercial fishing industries ($2 billion annually). The Alaska Department of Fish and Game regulates seasons, quotas, and gear for all commercial species including salmon, halibut, crab, and pollock. Commercial fishers must obtain limited entry permits (IFQ, CDQ, or permits). The North Pacific Fishery Management Council sets federal rules for offshore waters.
laws.penalty: Commercial fishing violations: fines up to $50,000, vessel forfeiture, and permit suspension.
laws.exceptions: Subsistence fishing by rural residents follows separate, non-commercial regulations.

quiz.q: What agency manages Alaska's commercial fisheries?
options: Alaska Dept. of Fish and Game
quiz.explanation: The Alaska Department of Fish and Game regulates Alaska's commercial fishing seasons, quotas, and permits.

laws.title: Internet Access in Rural Alaska
laws.subtitle: AS 44.21 — Alaska Broadband Task Force
laws.fullDescription: Alaska has some of the most significant digital divide challenges in the US, with many rural communities lacking broadband internet. The Alaska Broadband Task Force (2019) developed a statewide plan to expand access. State and federal funds support satellite and fixed wireless broadband deployment in underserved areas. Remote areas rely on USAC E-Rate and RDOF programs.
laws.penalty: N/A — this is a policy/infrastructure area.
laws.exceptions: Tribal lands may receive additional federal broadband support through FCC programs.

quiz.q: Does Alaska have a statewide broadband development plan?
options: Yes — Alaska Broadband Task Force plan
quiz.explanation: Alaska developed a statewide broadband plan through its Broadband Task Force to address the significant rural digital divide.

laws.title: Extreme Weather Child Safety Law
laws.subtitle: AS 47.17 — Child welfare in extreme conditions
laws.fullDescription: Alaska's extreme winter temperatures create unique child welfare concerns. Leaving a child in a car during extreme cold can be grounds for child neglect or endangerment charges. Alaska's Office of Children's Services has specific protocols for weather-related child welfare. During temperatures below -40°F, schools and agencies have emergency warming center requirements.
laws.penalty: Child neglect through exposure to extreme weather: class A misdemeanor to class C felony depending on harm caused.
laws.exceptions: Brief supervised periods for loading/unloading in vehicles are generally not prosecuted.

quiz.q: What is the consequence of leaving a child in a vehicle during extreme cold in Alaska?
quiz.explanation: Leaving a child in extreme cold in Alaska can result in child neglect or endangerment charges.

laws.title: Recreational Land Access Laws
laws.subtitle: AS 38.05 — Public access to state lands
laws.fullDescription: Alaska's vast public lands (state and federal) are generally open for recreational use including hunting, fishing, camping, and hiking. The Alaska Mental Health Trust Lands and other state lands may have specific access rules. The 'Alaska Public Easement Defense Act' protects traditional access routes across private land. Easements along navigable rivers are generally public.
laws.penalty: Trespassing on validly posted private land: class B misdemeanor.
laws.exceptions: Traditional trails and navigable waterways often have public easement protection even across private land.

quiz.q: Are traditional access routes across private land generally protected in Alaska?
options: Yes — public easement laws protect traditional routes
quiz.explanation: Alaska's Public Easement Defense Act and related laws protect traditional access routes even across private land.

laws.title: Youthful Offender Sentencing
laws.subtitle: AS 47.12 — Juvenile justice in Alaska
laws.fullDescription: Alaska has a separate juvenile justice system for offenders under 18. Juveniles may be tried as adults for serious crimes including murder, rape, and major felonies. The Division of Juvenile Justice operates youth correctional facilities. Alaska emphasizes rehabilitation over punishment for juvenile offenders, with restorative justice programs.
laws.penalty: Juvenile adjudications are not criminal convictions but can result in detention, probation, or treatment.
laws.exceptions: Juveniles 16+ charged with the most serious crimes (murder, sexual assault) may be waived to adult court.

quiz.q: Can juveniles be tried as adults in Alaska?
options: Yes, for serious crimes like murder and rape
quiz.explanation: Alaska allows juveniles to be tried as adults for serious crimes including murder and rape.

laws.title: Wildlife on Roadway Liability
laws.subtitle: AS 28 — Moose and wildlife collision rules
laws.fullDescription: Alaska has more wildlife-vehicle collisions than almost any other state, with moose being the primary concern. Hitting a moose or other large animal is generally treated as an at-fault accident unless the driver could not reasonably avoid it. Alaska State Troopers coordinate salvage of vehicle-killed moose for charitable food donation through the Alaska Moose Federation.
laws.penalty: Failure to report a large animal collision: potential traffic infraction fine.
laws.exceptions: Drivers who report collisions promptly and cooperate with salvage efforts face no further liability.

quiz.q: What happens to moose killed in vehicle collisions in Alaska?
options: Donated to charity through the Alaska Moose Federation
quiz.explanation: Alaska coordinates donation of vehicle-killed moose to charities through the Alaska Moose Federation.

laws.title: Alaska Tribal Child Welfare
laws.subtitle: ICWA + AS 47.10 — Indian Child Welfare Act
laws.fullDescription: Alaska has a high proportion of Alaska Native children in the foster care system. The Indian Child Welfare Act (ICWA) provides special protections for Native American children in custody proceedings, requiring placement preference with tribal relatives and tribal involvement in decisions. Alaska courts must follow ICWA for eligible children. Alaska also has state laws implementing ICWA.
laws.penalty: Failure to follow ICWA procedures can void custody orders.
laws.exceptions: Emergency removals for immediate safety may proceed before full ICWA procedures are completed.

quiz.q: What federal law provides special protections for Native American children in custody cases?
quiz.explanation: The Indian Child Welfare Act (ICWA) protects Alaska Native and other Native American children in custody proceedings.

laws.title: Village Public Safety Officers
laws.subtitle: AS 18.65.670 — VPSO program
laws.fullDescription: Alaska's Village Public Safety Officer (VPSO) program provides law enforcement presence in rural communities that cannot support full police departments. VPSOs are not sworn peace officers but provide emergency response, fire prevention, and search and rescue services. They are funded jointly by the state and tribal organizations. Many rural villages have no other law enforcement.
laws.penalty: N/A — this defines a law enforcement program, not a criminal law.
laws.exceptions: VPSOs operate under the supervision of Alaska State Troopers for law enforcement matters.

quiz.q: What type of law enforcement serves remote Alaska villages where state troopers aren't present?
quiz.explanation: Village Public Safety Officers (VPSOs) provide emergency response and law enforcement support in remote Alaska communities.

laws.title: Jones Act (Cabotage) Impact on Alaska
laws.subtitle: Federal 46 USC 55102 — Jones Act shipping
laws.fullDescription: The federal Jones Act (Merchant Marine Act of 1920) requires goods shipped between US ports to be carried by US-built, US-flagged, and US-crewed vessels. For Alaska, which receives most goods by sea, this significantly raises costs — some estimates put the premium at $400–$1 billion/year. Alaska has long lobbied for Jones Act reform to reduce cost of living in remote communities.
laws.penalty: N/A — this is a federal shipping law, not a state criminal law.
laws.exceptions: Some emergency waivers of the Jones Act have been issued by the President in crisis situations.

quiz.q: Why does the Jones Act significantly affect Alaska's cost of living?
options: It requires goods shipped between US ports to use US vessels, raising shipping costs
quiz.explanation: The Jones Act requires costly US vessels for shipping between US ports, significantly raising Alaska's cost of living since most goods arrive by sea.

laws.title: Remote Location Disclosure in Real Estate
laws.subtitle: AS 34.70 — Alaska Sellers Disclosure Act
laws.fullDescription: Alaska's Sellers Disclosure Act requires home sellers to disclose known material defects and conditions. In Alaska, this includes unique factors like permafrost conditions, flood plain status, access road conditions (seasonal or year-round), distance from emergency services, and water/sewer type (municipal, well, septic). Remote property buyers must be informed of all materially relevant conditions.
laws.penalty: Seller non-disclosure of material defects: buyer may rescind the sale or seek damages.
laws.exceptions: Foreclosure sales and estate sales may have reduced disclosure requirements.

quiz.q: Must Alaska sellers disclose permafrost conditions under the disclosure act?
options: Yes — permafrost is a material condition requiring disclosure
quiz.explanation: Alaska's seller disclosure requirements include permafrost conditions, which can significantly affect property stability and value.

laws.title: Volcanic Hazard Awareness Law
laws.subtitle: AS 46.17 — Natural disaster preparedness
laws.fullDescription: Alaska has more active volcanoes than any other US state (over 130). The Alaska Volcano Observatory (AVO) monitors volcanic activity and issues alerts. Emergency management plans are required for communities near active volcanoes. Ash fall can disrupt air traffic statewide. During eruptions, air quality and road safety laws apply.
laws.penalty: Failure to follow evacuation orders during volcanic eruptions: class B misdemeanor (emergency management laws).
laws.exceptions: Essential workers and first responders are exempt from evacuation orders.

quiz.q: How many active volcanoes does Alaska have?
quiz.explanation: Alaska has over 130 active volcanoes — more than any other US state.

laws.title: Permafrost Protection Regulations
laws.subtitle: AS 46.03 — Land use and permafrost
laws.fullDescription: Permafrost (permanently frozen ground) underlies about 80% of Alaska. Construction in permafrost zones requires special engineering to avoid thaw settlement. DEC and DNR regulations require permafrost assessments for construction projects. Climate change-induced permafrost thaw is creating major infrastructure challenges across Alaska.
laws.penalty: Construction without required permafrost assessment: stop-work orders and civil fines.
laws.exceptions: Small structures and some rural cabin construction have reduced engineering requirements.

quiz.q: What percentage of Alaska is underlain by permafrost?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 80% of Alaska is underlain by permafrost, requiring special construction techniques.

laws.title: Oil Industry Worker Protections
laws.subtitle: AS 23.10 — Industry-specific safety rules
laws.fullDescription: Alaska's oil and gas industry workers (especially on the North Slope) have specific protections including mandatory rest periods, extreme cold weather safety protocols, and remote location emergency plans. Workers must complete specific safety training before working on the slope. Alaska OSHA enforces workplace safety, with additional requirements for arctic environments.
laws.penalty: OSHA violations in oil industry: fines up to $15,625 per violation; repeat violations up to $156,259.
laws.exceptions: Contractors may have slightly different regulations than direct employees in some cases.

quiz.q: What unique safety requirements exist for Alaska North Slope oil workers?
options: Mandatory rest periods and cold weather safety protocols
quiz.explanation: Alaska North Slope workers have mandatory rest periods and extreme cold weather safety protocols beyond standard OSHA requirements.

laws.title: Alaska Native Sovereignty & Tribal Law
laws.subtitle: AS 01.10 + Federal law — Tribal legal authority
laws.fullDescription: Alaska Native tribes have limited sovereign authority, including jurisdiction over tribal members on tribal lands and authority to operate tribal courts for family law and civil matters. ANCSA (1971) extinguished most Alaska Native land claims but tribes retain governmental status. Federal Recognition of 229 Alaska Native tribes gives them certain protections and authorities.
laws.penalty: N/A — this defines jurisdictional boundaries between state, federal, and tribal law.
laws.exceptions: Criminal jurisdiction over non-Natives on tribal lands is primarily federal and state, not tribal.

quiz.q: How many federally recognized Alaska Native tribes are there?
quiz.explanation: There are 229 federally recognized Alaska Native tribes in Alaska.

laws.title: FAA Pilot License Requirements
laws.subtitle: Federal FAA + AS 02 — Aviation in Alaska
laws.fullDescription: Alaska has more pilots per capita than any other state. Private pilots must hold at least a Private Pilot Certificate from the FAA. Flying in Alaska requires specific mountain flying and backcountry training not required elsewhere. Many Alaska pilots hold seaplane ratings (Single Engine Sea). Fly-in communities are common and aviation is essential for rural access.
laws.penalty: Flying without a valid pilot certificate: federal felony; reckless flying: up to 1 year in federal prison.
laws.exceptions: Student pilots may fly solo with proper endorsements from certified flight instructors.

quiz.q: Does Alaska have more pilots per capita than any other US state?
quiz.explanation: Alaska has more pilots per capita than any other state — aviation is essential for accessing remote communities.

laws.title: Alaska Dental Health Aide Therapist
laws.subtitle: AS 08.36 — Dental therapist authorization
laws.fullDescription: Alaska became the first US state to authorize Dental Health Aide Therapists (DHAT) in 2005 — mid-level dental providers who can perform basic dental procedures in remote communities without a supervising dentist present. This was pioneered to address severe dental care shortages in rural Alaska Native communities. DHATs practice in village dental clinics under Tribal Health Organizations.
laws.penalty: Practicing beyond authorized scope: disciplinary action by the Dental Board.
laws.exceptions: DHAT practice is limited to tribal health settings — they cannot practice in mainstream dental offices.

quiz.q: Alaska was the first US state to authorize which type of mid-level dental provider?
quiz.explanation: Alaska pioneered the Dental Health Aide Therapist (DHAT) program in 2005 to provide dental care in remote communities.

laws.title: Marijuana Concentrate Regulations
laws.subtitle: AS 17.38.090 — Cannabis concentrate rules
laws.fullDescription: Alaska regulates cannabis concentrates (hash, wax, shatter, vape pens) similarly to flower, with adults 21+ permitted to possess up to 1 gram of concentrate. Retail stores may sell concentrates from licensed manufacturers. Home extraction using flammable solvents (like butane) is illegal for safety reasons. Licensed facilities use approved extraction methods.
laws.penalty: Home butane hash oil (BHO) extraction: class C felony for creating a fire/explosion hazard.
laws.exceptions: Licensed commercial extractors using approved methods are exempt.

quiz.q: Why is home cannabis concentrate extraction using butane illegal in Alaska?
options: Only licensed users can possess concentrates
quiz.explanation: Home butane hash oil (BHO) extraction is illegal in Alaska because it creates a dangerous fire and explosion hazard.

laws.title: Salmon Stream Buffer Law
laws.subtitle: AS 41.17.120 — Stream habitat protection
laws.fullDescription: Alaska's Forest Practices Act establishes riparian buffer zones (required setbacks) around salmon streams to protect habitat from logging and development. These 'buffer strips' vary from 50 to 100 feet depending on stream size and classification. Violations can affect both commercial logging permits and development approvals.
laws.penalty: Logging or development within protected buffer zones: permit revocation, restoration orders, and civil fines.
laws.exceptions: Certain maintenance, restoration, and limited access work may be allowed within buffer zones with permit.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of riparian buffer zones around Alaska salmon streams?
options: Salmon habitat protection from logging and development
quiz.explanation: Alaska's buffer zones around salmon streams protect fish habitat from logging, development, and runoff.

laws.title: North Slope Oil Development Rules
laws.subtitle: AS 38.05.180 — Oil and gas leasing regulations
laws.fullDescription: Alaska's North Slope (including Prudhoe Bay, the nation's largest oil field) is subject to extensive state and federal regulations governing exploration, extraction, and pipeline operation. The Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission oversees well operations. Environmental impact assessments are required for major new developments including ANWR and Willow Project approvals.
laws.penalty: Regulatory violations on state oil leases: fines up to $100,000/day plus potential lease revocation.
laws.exceptions: Emergency production decisions may bypass normal review timelines with state approval.

quiz.q: What state agency oversees well operations on Alaska's North Slope?
options: Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission
quiz.explanation: The Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission (AOGCC) oversees oil and gas well operations in Alaska.

laws.title: Public Land Camping Rules
laws.subtitle: AS 38.05 — State land camping regulations
laws.fullDescription: Alaska allows camping on most state and federal public lands with some restrictions. Many areas require no permit for dispersed camping. National Parks (Denali, Katmai, etc.) have their own permit systems for backcountry camping. State campgrounds in parks charge fees. Leave No Trace principles are strongly encouraged and some fragile areas have specific waste disposal requirements.
laws.penalty: Violating camping regulations in restricted areas: up to $1,000 fine; damage to protected land can result in civil restoration costs.
laws.exceptions: Alaska Native subsistence and traditional land use practices have separate provisions.

quiz.q: Do most Alaska public lands require a permit for dispersed camping?
options: No — most allow permit-free dispersed camping
quiz.explanation: Most Alaska public lands allow dispersed camping without a permit, though national parks have their own backcountry permit systems.
